title: Bathroom Vanity Storage Solutions: Organize Drawers, Under the Sink and Countertop
excerpt: Bathroom vanity storage solutions for drawers, the cabinet under the sink, the countertop and nearby walls, plus what not to store in a vanity and how to choose one.
content: The bathroom vanity does more work than almost any other piece of furniture in the home. It holds the sink, hides the plumbing, and stores everything from toothpaste and hair tools to cleaning supplies and spare toilet paper. When it is disorganized, mornings slow down and the countertop disappears under bottles. The right **bathroom vanity storage solutions** give each item a home inside the drawers, behind the doors, on the counter and on the wall nearby.

This guide covers the whole vanity, not only the cabinet under the sink: drawer organization, under-sink systems, countertop storage, the walls and mirror around the vanity, what should not be stored there, and what to look for if you are choosing a new vanity. For deep dives on the cabinet below the basin, see our [under bathroom sink organization ideas](/blog/under-bathroom-sink-organization-ideas) and [best under-sink organizers for bathrooms](/blog/best-under-sink-organizers-bathrooms-review-buying-guide-2026).

Hero photo credit: [Tomwsulcer](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bathroom_vanity_cabinet_including_sink_and_drawers.jpg) / Wikimedia Commons, [CC0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/)
## Start With an Audit of Your Vanity

Before buying organizers, empty the vanity completely. Wipe every drawer and shelf and check the cabinet floor for water stains or soft spots, which can mean a slow leak at the trap or supply lines. Then sort what you removed into groups: daily essentials, weekly items, backups, cleaning products, and things that do not belong in the bathroom at all.
Throw away expired products, dried-out makeup and empty bottles. Combine duplicates. You will usually find that a vanity has more space than it seemed; it was simply filled with things nobody uses.
Measure the inside of each drawer and the cabinet below the sink, including the height and width around the drain pipe. These numbers decide which organizers will fit.
## Map the Vanity Into Zones
Zoning keeps a vanity organized long after the first clean-out. Each part of the vanity gets one job, based on how often you use the items.

![Diagram of a bathroom vanity divided into zones: daily essentials in the top drawer, hair tools and grooming items in the second drawer, cleaning supplies and backups under the sink around the pipes, a small tray on the countertop, and a wall shelf beside the mirror](/images/blog/bathroom-vanity-storage-solutions-zone-diagram.svg)
| Vanity zone | What to store | Best organizer | Tip |
| Top drawer | Toothbrush, toothpaste, skincare, deodorant | Clear divider trays | Keep only daily items here |
| Second drawer | Hair tools, brushes, grooming kits | Deep bins, heat-safe holder | Let hot tools cool before storing |
| Under the sink | Cleaning supplies, backups, paper goods | Two-tier pull-out organizer | Leave room around pipes and valves |
| Countertop | Hand soap, one tray of daily items | Small tray or caddy | Keep at least half the counter clear |
| Wall beside mirror | Towels, decor, extra toiletries | Floating shelf, towel bar | Use waterproof finishes |
| Inside cabinet doors | Small tools, cloths, hair ties | Adhesive hooks, door rack | Check that doors still close |
## Drawer Organization That Lasts
Drawers are the most efficient part of a vanity because you can see everything from above. Without dividers, though, they turn into a jumble within days.

![Diagram of a vanity top drawer seen from above, divided with trays of different sizes: toothbrush and toothpaste at the front, skincare bottles standing upright, a small lidded box for hair ties and pins, and cotton pads at the back](/images/blog/bathroom-vanity-storage-solutions-drawer-layout.svg)

Use modular trays in several sizes so you can build a layout that fits your drawer exactly. Clear trays make it easy to see what is inside and wipe up spills. Small lidded boxes are useful for loose items such as hair ties, bobby pins and cotton swabs.

![Clear plastic storage boxes with snap lids holding small items such as clips and colorful accessories on a desk. Photo: Sesoris product catalog](/images/blog/bathroom-vanity-storage-solutions-clear-boxes.webp)

A set of [Clear Plastic Storage Boxes](/product/clear-plastic-storage-boxes-24-pack) works well for this, because the lids keep tiny items from scattering when the drawer slams. For makeup and skincare collections, our [makeup organization ideas](/blog/makeup-organization-ideas) show how to sort by product type.
Store items standing up where you can. Upright tubes and bottles are easier to grab and take less space than items lying flat. Keep the front of the drawer for what you use most often.
## Under-Sink Storage Around the Plumbing

The cabinet under the sink is the trickiest part of the vanity because the drain pipe cuts through the middle. Two-tier pull-out organizers solve this well: they slide out like drawers, so nothing gets lost at the back, and many are designed to fit beside the pipes.
![Black two-tier pull-out wire organizer with sliding baskets holding white bottles and sponges. Photo: Sesoris product catalog](/images/blog/bathroom-vanity-storage-solutions-pull-out.webp)

A narrow unit such as the [Pull-Out Under-Sink Organizer, 2 Tiers](/product/pull-out-under-sink-organizer-2-tier-black) can sit on each side of the drain. Use the bottom tier for heavier items such as refill bottles and the top tier for lighter ones such as sponges and cloths. If you prefer a custom approach, our tutorial on [building a DIY under-sink storage system](/blog/how-to-build-diy-under-sink-storage-system-step-by-step-tutorial-2026) walks through it step by step.

Leave space around the shutoff valves so you can reach them quickly in a leak. A washable mat or shallow tray on the cabinet floor catches drips and protects the wood. If children live in your home, add a child-safety latch to the cabinet doors whenever cleaning products are stored there.
## What Not to Store in a Bathroom Vanity

Some items do better outside the bathroom. Medicine is the most important example. MedlinePlus, the National Library of Medicine's consumer health site, explains in its guide to [storing your medicines](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/patientinstructions/000534.htm) that the heat and moisture from your shower, bath and sink may damage medicines. It recommends a cool, dry place such as a dresser drawer or a kitchen cabinet away from the stove, sink and hot appliances, always out of reach and out of sight of children.
Other items to keep elsewhere:
- **Spare towels and linens** in large quantities, which belong in a linen closet. See our [ideas for linen closet organization](/blog/ideas-for-linen-closet-organization).
- **Paper products in bulk**, which can absorb humidity.
- **Jewelry and watches**, which can tarnish in steam.
- **Anything that is not used in the bathroom**, which simply takes space from what is.
## Countertop Storage Without Clutter
A clear countertop makes a bathroom look larger and makes cleaning faster. The goal is not an empty counter, but a contained one.
1. **Use one tray.** Gather daily items such as hand soap, a toothbrush cup and one skincare bottle on a single tray. Everything outside the tray goes in a drawer.
2. **Choose matching dispensers.** Refill soap and lotion into simple pumps to reduce visual noise.
3. **Go vertical on the counter.** A small tiered stand holds more in the same footprint.
4. **Keep hot tools off the counter.** Store a hair dryer and straightener in a heat-safe holder inside a cabinet once they cool.
## Store Hair Tools Safely

Hair dryers, straighteners and curling irons are some of the bulkiest items in a vanity, and their cords tangle everything around them. They also stay hot for a while after use, so a little planning keeps them both tidy and safe.
1. **Let tools cool completely** on a heat-resistant mat on the counter before you put them away.
2. **Give them their own spot.** A deep drawer or a holder mounted inside a cabinet door keeps tools upright and separate from plastic bottles.
3. **Wrap cords loosely** and secure them with a reusable tie instead of winding them tightly around the tool, which can strain the cord over time.
4. **Keep tools away from the sink** while plugged in, and unplug them as soon as you finish.
5. **Store attachments with the tool** in a small bin so diffusers and nozzles do not wander.
## Organizing a Shared or Double Vanity

When two people share a vanity, the most effective storage solution is a clear division. Give each person their own drawer or their own side of the cabinet, and resist the temptation to mix daily items. Shared items, such as hand soap, toothpaste refills and cotton swabs, can sit in the middle or in one labeled bin that both people use.

Color coding helps, especially for children: one color of tray or cup per person makes it obvious where things go. If the vanity has one sink but two users, a two-level countertop caddy gives each person a level without spreading across the whole counter. Our [bathroom closet organization systems guide](/blog/bathroom-closet-organization-systems) shows how the same zoning idea works for backup supplies kept outside the vanity.
## Use the Walls Around the Vanity

When the vanity itself is full, the wall above and beside it can add a lot of storage. A shallow shelf above the faucet or beside the mirror holds everyday items without crowding the counter. A towel bar or ring at the side of the vanity keeps hand towels within reach.

A medicine cabinet or mirrored cabinet adds hidden storage at eye level; our [medicine cabinet organization ideas](/blog/medicine-cabinet-organization-ideas) cover how to sort it, though remember that it is still a humid spot for medicines themselves. For more options, browse our [bathroom wall shelf ideas](/blog/bathroom-wall-shelf-ideas-transform-space-2026) and [bathroom towel storage ideas](/blog/bathroom-towel-storage-ideas).
## Choosing a Vanity With Better Storage
If you are replacing a vanity, storage should be as important as style. Compare these features before you buy:
- **Drawers versus doors.** A vanity with several drawers is usually easier to keep organized than one large cabinet with doors.
- **U-shaped drawers** that wrap around the plumbing give drawer storage even below the sink.
- **Floating vanities** leave the floor open for a basket or step stool and make cleaning easier.
- **Open shelves** under the basin show off rolled towels but collect dust.
- **Moisture-resistant materials** and finishes hold up better in a steamy room.
- **Size and layout.** Measure the room, door swing and plumbing location, and choose the largest vanity that leaves comfortable clearance.
For a broader look at bathroom furniture, see our [bathroom cabinet ideas](/blog/bathroom-cabinet-ideas) and [bathroom storage cabinet ideas](/blog/bathroom-storage-cabinet-ideas).
## Small Bathroom Vanity Storage Solutions
In a small bathroom, every inch counts. Pedestal sinks and narrow vanities leave little room, so storage has to move up and out.
- **Add a slim cart** beside the vanity for daily items.
- **Use the inside of cabinet doors** for adhesive hooks and slim racks.
- **Stack drawer trays** where the drawer is deep enough.
- **Mount a shelf above the toilet** for backups.
- **Keep only what you use**, and store the rest in a hall closet.

Our [small bathroom storage ideas](/blog/small-bathroom-storage-ideas) and [storage space ideas for small bathrooms](/blog/storage-space-ideas-for-small-bathroom-maximize-every-inch-2026) have more space-saving fixes.
## Keep Your Vanity Organized

A good system only lasts if it is easy to maintain. Give every item a home, put things back right after use, and do a quick reset once a week: return strays, wipe drips and refill soap. Every few months, check expiration dates, clear out products you no longer use and look under the sink for any signs of leaks.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Bathroom Vanity Storage Solutions
**Q: How do I organize a bathroom vanity with no drawers?**

Add pull-out organizers or stackable bins inside the cabinet so items slide forward instead of getting lost at the back, use the inside of the doors for hooks or slim racks, and keep a small tray on the counter for daily essentials.
**Q: What is the best way to store things under a bathroom sink?**
Use two-tier pull-out organizers that fit around the drain pipe, keep the shutoff valves accessible, put a washable mat or tray on the cabinet floor and store heavier items on the bottom tier.
**Q: Should I keep medicine in my bathroom vanity?**

It is better not to. MedlinePlus explains that heat and moisture from the shower, bath and sink can damage medicines and recommends a cool, dry place such as a dresser drawer or a kitchen cabinet, out of reach of children.
**Q: How can I add storage to a small bathroom vanity?**
Use drawer dividers, stack trays in deep drawers, add door hooks, place a slim cart beside the vanity and use wall shelves above the counter or toilet.
**Q: What should go in the top drawer of a vanity?**
Only daily essentials such as your toothbrush, toothpaste, skincare and deodorant, sorted into clear divider trays so each item has a fixed spot.
**Q: How do I keep my bathroom countertop clutter-free?**
Gather daily items on a single tray, use matching dispensers, store hot tools in a cabinet once they cool and move everything else into drawers.
**Q: What type of vanity offers the most storage?**
Vanities with multiple drawers, especially U-shaped drawers that wrap around the plumbing, usually make the best use of space and are easier to keep organized than a single cabinet with doors.
**Q: How often should I clean out my bathroom vanity?**
Do a quick reset weekly and a full clean-out every few months to remove expired products and check for leaks under the sink.
## Conclusion: A Vanity That Works Every Morning

The best bathroom vanity storage solutions start with an honest clean-out and a simple map: daily items in the top drawer, tools in the second, cleaning supplies and backups under the sink, one tray on the counter and extra storage on the wall. Keep medicines elsewhere, leave the plumbing accessible and reset weekly. Your mornings will feel calmer for it.
